
Which content structure is correct?
options: [{"imageUrl": "data:image/jpeg;base64,..."}, {"text": "What defect is shown?"}]
"<image>...base64...</image> What defect is shown?"
[{"image": {"format": "jpeg", "source": {"bytes": img_bytes}}}, {"text": "What defect is shown?"}]
[{"text": "What defect is shown?"}] with the image passed in inferenceConfig={"image": img_bytes}
optionExplanations: Converse has no imageUrl/data-URI field; images are passed as image blocks with raw bytes, not as URLs.
Converse does not accept an image embedded in a raw text string with pseudo-tags.
Correct: a Converse image block uses a format and a source carrying raw bytes (source.bytes), alongside a text block in the content list.
Images are never passed via inferenceConfig; multimodal input belongs in the message content list.
explanation: Converse multimodal content uses an image block with a format and a source carrying raw bytes (source.bytes), alongside a text block, in the content list. Converse does not use an imageUrl/data-URI field, does not accept images embedded in a raw string, and images are never passed via inferenceConfig.

question: You send 12 high-resolution site photos plus a long spec PDF in one Converse request and hit throughput/context pressure. Which statement about multimodal token budgeting is accurate?
options: Images are free; only text blocks consume input tokens, so image count never affects the context budget.
Each image consumes input tokens roughly proportional to its dimensions/resolution, so downsizing images and sending fewer per request reduces token usage and helps stay within the context window.
Documents are converted to a single token regardless of length, so PDF size is irrelevant.
Multimodal blocks are billed as output tokens, not input tokens.
optionExplanations: Images are not free—they consume input tokens proportional to resolution/size, so image count does affect the context budget.
Correct — each image costs input tokens roughly proportional to its dimensions/resolution, so downsizing and sending fewer per request reduces token usage.
Documents are tokenized by their extracted text content, not collapsed to a single token, so PDF length very much matters.
Multimodal inputs are billed as input tokens, not output tokens.
explanation: Images cost input tokens scaling with resolution/size, and documents are tokenized by their text content, so both count against the input context budget; downsizing and trimming images (and splitting requests) is the practical fix. Images are not free (A), documents are not one token (C), and multimodal inputs are billed as input, not output, tokens (D).

question: You want each S3 document to carry filterable attributes (project, docType) usable in retrieval filters. How do you attach this metadata for a Bedrock Knowledge Base S3 data source?
options: Embed the attributes as the first line of each PDF's text and Bedrock will parse them into filters.
Pass a metadata dict in the retrieve call; ingestion metadata is not supported.
Set S3 object tags only; Bedrock reads tags as filter metadata automatically.

Place a companion <filename>.metadata.json sidecar next to each object containing a metadataAttributes object, then run an ingestion job so the attributes are indexed and become usable in filter expressions.
optionExplanations: Wrong: attributes placed in the PDF body text are not parsed into filterable metadata by Bedrock.
Wrong: ingestion-time metadata is supported and filters operate on it; you do not supply filter metadata as a dict in the retrieve call.
Wrong: Bedrock does not read S3 object tags as filter metadata for Knowledge Bases.
Correct: place a <filename>.metadata.json sidecar with a metadataAttributes object next to each object, then run an ingestion job so the attributes are indexed and usable in filters.
explanation: For S3 sources you attach a <filename>.metadata.json sidecar with metadataAttributes, then run ingestion so the attributes are indexed and filterable (D). Attributes in body text are not parsed into filters (A), filters operate on ingested metadata rather than being supplied only at query time (B), and S3 object tags are not the metadata mechanism for Knowledge Bases (C).

question:
During distillation you notice the teacher's synthesized responses are what the student learns from. Given:

```python
customizationConfig={"distillationConfig": {"teacherModelConfig": {
    "teacherModelIdentifier": TEACHER,
    "maxResponseLengthForInference": 512}}}
```

What does maxResponseLengthForInference control and why does it matter for distillation quality?
options: It caps the length of the teacher's generated responses used as training targets; too small truncates the labels the student learns, hurting quality on long-form tasks.
It sets the student's maximum output length at deployment time.
It limits the number of training prompts processed.
It is the maximum sequence length of the input prompts, rejecting longer ones.
optionExplanations: Correct: it caps the length of the teacher's generated responses used as training targets, so setting it too low truncates those labels and hurts the student on long-form tasks.
Wrong: it bounds the teacher's label-generation length during training, not the student's maximum output length at deployment time.
Wrong: it governs generated response length, not the number of training prompts processed.
Wrong: it limits generated response length, not input prompt sequence length, and does not reject over-length prompts.
explanation: maxResponseLengthForInference bounds how long the teacher's generated answers (the distillation labels) can be; setting it too low truncates the very targets the student imitates, degrading long-form performance. It governs teacher outputs during label synthesis, not the student's deployment output length, the prompt count, or input truncation.

question: A guardrail is attached in your wrapper, but a pen test shows a user can still get disallowed content by calling InvokeModel directly (bypassing the wrapper that adds guardrailConfig). What is the correct architectural fix?
options: Publish a new guardrail version so it applies globally to the account's InvokeModel calls
Set the guardrail to DRAFT so it enforces on all calls automatically
Add an IAM condition (bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier) so InvokeModel is denied unless the matching guardrail is attached to the request
Rely on the model provider's built-in alignment instead of a guardrail
optionExplanations: Wrong: publishing a new guardrail version creates an immutable snapshot but does not make the guardrail auto-apply to the account's InvokeModel calls; guardrails are per-request.
Wrong: DRAFT is just the mutable working copy and does not enforce automatically on all calls; it has no global-enforcement effect.

Correct: guardrails are per-request, so enforcement is made mandatory via an IAM condition (bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier) that denies InvokeModel unless the matching guardrail is attached, closing the bypass.
Wrong: relying on the provider's built-in alignment is not a substitute for an enforced guardrail and cannot close the direct-InvokeModel bypass.
explanation: Guardrails are per-request, not account-global, so enforcement must be made mandatory via IAM: denying InvokeModel unless the request carries the required guardrail (bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier condition) closes the bypass. Publishing a version does not make it auto-apply (A wrong). DRAFT is just a working copy, not a global enforcement switch (B wrong). Provider alignment is not a substitute for enforced guardrails (D wrong).

question: A production endpoint invoking Anthropic Claude in us-east-1 begins returning ThrottlingException during daily traffic peaks, even though the account is well under its overall service quota. The team wants higher sustained throughput without reserving dedicated capacity and can tolerate requests being served from other Regions in the same geography. What should they use?
options: An on-demand cross-region inference profile so requests are automatically routed across Regions in the geography for higher throughput and resilience
A single-Region Provisioned Throughput reservation pinned to us-east-1
Batch inference jobs to spread the load over time
A latency-optimized inference profile to remove throttling
optionExplanations: Correct: an on-demand cross-region (system-defined) inference profile distributes traffic across the Regions in its geography, raising effective throughput and resilience with no reserved capacity.
Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated capacity (and cost) in one Region — the opposite of 'without reserving dedicated capacity'.
Batch inference is asynchronous and does not help a real-time endpoint's peak throughput.
Latency-optimized inference reduces response latency on supported models; it does not add cross-Region capacity to relieve throttling.
explanation: Cross-region inference profiles route on-demand requests across the Regions in a geography, increasing sustained throughput and availability without a capacity reservation. Requests may be processed in any Region within the profile's geography. Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity in a single Region, batch is asynchronous, and latency-optimized inference targets latency, not throttling.

question: During a Converse tool-use exchange, the model returns a response with stopReason 'tool_use' containing a toolUse block that names a function and its input. What must the application do next to continue the conversation correctly?
options: Execute the requested tool, then send the result back as a toolResult content block in a new user message and call Converse again
Ignore the block and re-send the original prompt with a higher temperature
Return the toolUse block unchanged as the assistant's final answer
Switch to InvokeModel because Converse cannot complete tool calls
optionExplanations: Correct: the app runs the tool, wraps the output in a toolResult (referencing the toolUseId) inside a user-role message, and calls Converse again so the model can use the result.
Re-sending the prompt discards the tool request and breaks the tool-use loop.
A toolUse block is a request for data, not a final answer to surface to the user.
Converse fully supports the tool-use loop; switching APIs is unnecessary.
explanation: The tool-use loop: model emits toolUse with stopReason 'tool_use' → app executes the tool → app returns a toolResult (matching toolUseId) in a user message → Converse is called again so the model incorporates the result.

question: A Knowledge Base indexes long policy manuals. Retrieved chunks frequently cut sentences mid-thought and lose surrounding context, degrading answer quality. Which change most directly addresses this at ingestion time?
options: Adjust the chunking strategy — e.g., semantic or hierarchical chunking, or larger chunks with overlap — so retrieved segments preserve context
Lower the model temperature during generation
Switch the generation model to a larger one
Increase the number of results returned (topK) without changing chunking
optionExplanations: Correct: chunking strategy determines how documents are split; semantic/hierarchical chunking or larger overlapping chunks keep context intact.
Temperature affects generation randomness, not how source text was split during ingestion.
A bigger generation model cannot recover context that was lost when the source was fragmented.
Returning more fragmented chunks adds noise without fixing the underlying fragmentation.
explanation: Context loss from mid-sentence splits is a chunking problem solved at ingestion. Bedrock Knowledge Bases support fixed, semantic, and hierarchical chunking (plus overlap); choosing a context-preserving strategy is the direct fix.

question: A Bedrock Agent must be able to look up order status by calling an existing internal REST service during a conversation. What is the standard way to give the agent this capability?
options: Define an action group with an API/function schema, backed by a Lambda function that calls the internal service
Paste the API documentation into the agent's instructions and hope it calls the endpoint
Enable Provisioned Throughput on the agent
Attach a Guardrail that forwards requests to the service
optionExplanations: Correct: action groups define the operations (via OpenAPI/function schema) and are fulfilled by a Lambda function (or return of control) that performs the call.
Instructions alone cannot make the agent invoke an external service; there is no execution path.
Provisioned Throughput is a capacity mode and does not grant tool/API capabilities.
Guardrails filter content for safety; they do not execute API calls.
explanation: Bedrock Agents call external systems through action groups: you declare operations with a schema and back them with a Lambda function that performs the work (or use return of control to let your app execute).

question: Across several applications and models, a company must consistently block disallowed topics, filter hate/violence content, and redact PII from both prompts and responses. Which Bedrock capability provides this reusable policy layer?
options: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, which can be attached to model calls or applied via ApplyGuardrail to filter content, denied topics, and PII
IAM policies scoped to model ARNs
A VPC interface endpoint
Model invocation logging
optionExplanations: Correct: Guardrails enforce content filters, denied topics, word filters, and PII handling, and can be reused across models and applications.
IAM controls who can invoke which models; it does not inspect or filter prompt/response content.
A VPC endpoint controls network path privacy, not content safety.
Invocation logging records requests/responses for audit; it does not block or redact content.
explanation: Bedrock Guardrails provide a reusable responsible-AI policy layer (content filters, denied topics, word/PII filters, contextual grounding). They can be attached to Converse/InvokeModel or applied independently with ApplyGuardrail across models.

question: A nightly pipeline must summarize roughly two million archived documents stored in Amazon S3. Latency per item is irrelevant, but cost matters and the job should not compete with the interactive API traffic. Which Bedrock capability best fits?
options: Batch inference via CreateModelInvocationJob, reading input from S3 and writing results back to S3 at a lower per-token price
A high concurrency of on-demand InvokeModel calls
ConverseStream to overlap generation with processing
Provisioned Throughput sized for two million requests
optionExplanations: Correct: batch inference processes large S3 datasets asynchronously at a discounted price and runs separately from real-time traffic.
Flooding on-demand InvokeModel would risk throttling and compete with interactive traffic at full price.
Streaming only changes how a single response is delivered; it does not address large asynchronous batch workloads or cost.
Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for steady real-time load and is not the cost-optimal path for a one-off bulk job.
explanation: Bedrock batch inference (CreateModelInvocationJob) is designed for large, latency-insensitive datasets in S3, runs asynchronously, and is offered at a lower price than on-demand — ideal for bulk offline summarization.

question: A model intermittently returns answers in prose when the downstream parser requires a strict JSON object. Instructions alone have not fixed it. Which prompt-engineering technique most reliably enforces the exact output shape?
options: Provide few-shot examples that each show input paired with the exact desired JSON output
Increase temperature so the model explores more formats
Remove the system prompt to avoid conflicting guidance
Ask the model to 'try harder to use JSON' at the end of the prompt
optionExplanations: Correct: concrete few-shot examples demonstrating the precise JSON shape strongly bias the model toward that format.
Higher temperature increases variability, making format drift more likely, not less.
Removing the system prompt discards useful constraints and rarely improves formatting.
Vague pleading is far less effective than showing exemplars of the required structure.
explanation: Few-shot prompting — showing several input→output pairs in the exact target format — is the most dependable way to lock in a structured output shape, especially combined with a low temperature.

question: A team replaces the embedding model used for their vector index with a newer one that produces different-dimension vectors. Queries now return irrelevant results. What is the required corrective action?
options: Re-embed and re-index the entire corpus with the new model so document and query embeddings come from the same model
Keep the old document vectors and only switch the query-time model
Pad the old vectors with zeros to match the new dimensions
Lower the similarity threshold to accept more matches
optionExplanations: Correct: query and document vectors must be produced by the same embedding model; changing models requires rebuilding the whole index.
Mixing an old document space with a new query model yields incomparable vectors and poor retrieval.
Zero-padding does not map old vectors into the new model's semantic space; results stay wrong.
Loosening the threshold surfaces more irrelevant matches rather than fixing the space mismatch.
explanation: Embeddings are only comparable within the same model's vector space. Switching embedding models invalidates existing vectors, so you must re-embed and re-index the full corpus with the new model.

question: A company has thousands of labeled prompt-and-ideal-response pairs and wants a base model to adopt their specific answer style and terminology. Which customization approach fits, and how does it differ from continued pre-training?
options: Fine-tuning on the labeled pairs; continued pre-training instead uses large amounts of unlabeled domain text
Continued pre-training on the labeled pairs; fine-tuning requires unlabeled text
Model distillation on the labeled pairs; it needs no data
RAG, because customization always means retrieval
optionExplanations: Correct: fine-tuning uses labeled prompt/completion examples to shape behavior/style; continued pre-training ingests large unlabeled corpora to add domain knowledge.
This reverses the definitions — fine-tuning is the labeled-data method.
Distillation transfers a teacher model's behavior and requires data; it is not the labeled-pairs style-adaptation method described.
RAG grounds answers with retrieved context but does not change the model's weights or inherent style.
explanation: Fine-tuning uses labeled examples (e.g., JSONL prompt/completion) to specialize style and behavior. Continued pre-training uses large unlabeled domain text to build knowledge. Both produce custom models needing Provisioned Throughput to invoke.

question: Compliance requires that data associated with a fine-tuning job and the resulting custom model be encrypted with a key the organization controls and can audit and revoke. What should be used?
options: A customer managed AWS KMS key (CMK) configured for the model customization job and custom model
The default AWS owned key with no configuration
Client-side base64 encoding of the training data
A VPC interface endpoint
optionExplanations: Correct: a customer managed KMS key lets the organization control, audit (via CloudTrail), rotate, and revoke access to the encryption key used for the job and custom model.
An AWS owned/managed key does not give the customer control, key policies, or revocation as required.
Base64 is an encoding, not encryption, and provides no confidentiality.
A VPC endpoint addresses network privacy, not encryption key ownership.
explanation: For customer-controlled encryption of customization jobs and custom models, configure a customer managed KMS key (CMK). This gives you key policies, rotation, auditability, and revocation that AWS owned keys do not.

question: An extraction service must return the same structured output for the same input as consistently as possible. Which inference parameter change most directly reduces randomness in the generated text?
options: Lower the temperature toward 0
Increase maxTokens
Raise top_p toward 1.0
Add more stop sequences
optionExplanations: Correct: temperature scales the randomness of sampling; lowering it toward 0 makes output more deterministic and repeatable.
maxTokens only caps output length; it does not affect determinism.
Raising top_p widens the candidate token pool, generally increasing variability rather than reducing it.
Stop sequences control where generation halts, not how random the sampled tokens are.
explanation: Determinism is governed chiefly by temperature (and secondarily top_p). Lowering temperature toward 0 minimizes randomness. maxTokens and stop sequences shape length/termination, not variability.

question: For a step in a workflow, the application must guarantee that the model calls a specific declared tool rather than answering directly or choosing another tool. Assuming the model supports it, how is this enforced in Converse?
options: Set toolChoice to require that specific tool by name
Delete all other tools from toolConfig for that request
Set temperature to 0 so the model is forced to call the tool
Add 'you must call the tool' only in the user message and hope the model complies
optionExplanations: Correct: toolChoice can be set to 'tool' with the tool's name to force that specific tool call on models that support toolChoice.
Removing other tools limits options but still does not guarantee the remaining tool is called rather than a text answer.
temperature affects sampling randomness, not whether a tool is invoked.
Natural-language insistence is not a guarantee; toolChoice is the explicit control.
explanation: toolChoice controls tool invocation: 'auto' (model decides), 'any' (must call some tool), or 'tool' with a name (must call that tool). To force a named tool, set toolChoice to that tool, on models that support it.

question: A multi-tenant RAG application must ensure that a query only retrieves passages belonging to the requesting tenant, even though all tenants share one Knowledge Base index. What is the appropriate mechanism?
options: Attach tenant metadata to documents at ingestion and apply a metadata filter on each retrieval request
Rely on a higher similarity threshold to exclude other tenants
Create a separate foundation model per tenant
Lower topK so fewer cross-tenant results appear
optionExplanations: Correct: document metadata plus a metadata filter at query time restricts retrieval to the matching tenant's passages.
Similarity thresholds rank by relevance, not ownership; they cannot enforce tenant isolation.
The foundation model does not control which passages are retrieved from the index.
Reducing topK just returns fewer results and still risks leaking other tenants' data.
explanation: Bedrock Knowledge Bases support attaching metadata to documents and applying metadata filters on Retrieve/RetrieveAndGenerate. Filtering on a tenant attribute enforces per-tenant retrieval isolation within a shared index.

question: Before launch, a team must compare two candidate models on their own dataset for accuracy and quality, using both automatic metrics and human reviewers. Which Bedrock feature supports this directly?
options: Bedrock model evaluation jobs, which offer automatic metrics and human (or LLM-as-a-judge) evaluation on your dataset
CloudWatch metrics for the endpoints
Provisioned Throughput benchmarking
Guardrails content filters
optionExplanations: Correct: Bedrock model evaluation lets you compare models on your dataset using automatic metrics, human review, or LLM-as-a-judge.
CloudWatch reports operational metrics (latency, invocations), not answer quality/accuracy on a dataset.
Provisioned Throughput concerns capacity, not evaluation of output quality.
Guardrails enforce safety policies; they do not benchmark model accuracy.
explanation: Bedrock model evaluation supports automatic metric-based jobs, human evaluation, and LLM-as-a-judge to compare models on a task dataset — the right tool for pre-launch quality/accuracy comparison.

question: Following least privilege, an IAM role for a service should be able to invoke only two approved foundation models and nothing else in Bedrock. How should the policy be written?
options: Grant bedrock:InvokeModel (and InvokeModelWithResponseStream) with Resource scoped to the two specific model ARNs
Grant bedrock:* on Resource '*' for simplicity
Grant bedrock:InvokeModel on Resource '*' and rely on a Guardrail to restrict models
Attach the AdministratorAccess managed policy to the role
optionExplanations: Correct: scoping bedrock:InvokeModel/InvokeModelWithResponseStream to the two model ARNs enforces least privilege on exactly the approved models.
bedrock:* on '*' grants far more than invoking two models, violating least privilege.
Guardrails do not restrict which models a principal may invoke; the Resource scope must do that.
AdministratorAccess is the opposite of least privilege.
explanation: Least privilege for model access is enforced with an IAM policy allowing bedrock:InvokeModel (and the streaming variant) on the specific model ARNs. Guardrails govern content, not which models an identity can call.
